source.title: How Well do Feature Visualizations Support Causal Understanding of CNN Activations?
source.authors: R. Zimmermann; Judy Borowski; Robert Geirhos; M. Bethge; Thomas S. A. Wallis; Wieland Brendel

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates how well people use visualizations to predict the effect of occlusions on InceptionV1 channel activations. It does not measure whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, feature superposition, or polysemanticity.
record.gate_note: The reported psychophysical results concern human prediction of activation changes, a related but different construct from the claim versions about neuron polysemanticity. The authors also describe a separate forward-simulation replication in Appendix A.3; it is not a test of polysemanticity.
record.test_reason: The study measures how accurately human raters predict occlusion effects on InceptionV1 channel activations given feature visualizations or dataset examples. It reports no measure of whether units respond to several unrelated inputs, and nothing on superposition, architecture effects or measurement dependence. It cites Zoom In only in passing: one unit may respond to different aspects, so diverse visualizations are hard. It neither tests nor uses polysemanticity, so it is T6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that Olah et al.'s feature visualizations help humans predict occlusion effects only modestly above no references, and no better than simpler alternatives such as dataset samples. Simple heuristic baselines reach a similar accuracy range (about 63%).
record.recipe_differences: The study uses Olah et al.-style feature visualizations as reference stimuli, but its method is a human psychophysical occlusion-prediction task rather than a measurement of neuron meanings or polysemanticity.
record.method_sensitivity: Human task performance varies with unit, query-image set, and the relative activation difference between the two occluded images; the activation-difference association is reported as stronger in the P OOL branch than in the 3×3 branch.

fits_no_version.finding: Human occlusion-prediction accuracy on InceptionV1 channels was 67±4% with synthetic feature visualizations, 60±3% with no references, and 66–67% with the other reference types. Accuracy varied strongly by unit: one layer-2 POOL unit was below chance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature visualizations give humans no more causal insight into CNN unit activations than natural dataset examples.

record.problems: The study samples units rather than testing all units, uses one network (InceptionV1), and constrains interventions to fixed-size square occlusions. The authors note that this limits how precisely occlusions can cover the image region responsible for activation.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix A.3's replication of a forward-simulation image-comparison task is not included: it is a separate task and does not measure neuron polysemanticity or the focal occlusion-prediction result.

untested.parts: Whether InceptionV1 units respond to several unrelated inputs. The paper only notes that some units have unclear selectivity (Fig. 6B).
Language-model MLP neurons; none are studied.
Superposition as the cause of polysemanticity.
Dependence on architecture, activation function or regularization.
Whether mixed responses reflect one shared feature.
Dependence on activation range or explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: Relation is changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': Zoom In is cited only in passing, for units responding to different aspects. The human-rater rows are not polysemanticity measures. The abstract and the body differ slightly on the synthetic-reference accuracy (68±4% vs 67±4%) and on the upper end of the alternatives' range (67±3% vs 67±5%).

versions.untested_parts: Whether individual image-classifier neurons respond strongly to several unrelated kinds of input.
Language-model MLP neurons and unrelated tokens or contexts.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Changes in polysemanticity across architectures, activations, or regularization, including performance costs.
Whether apparently mixed neuron responses share a coherent feature or job.
Whether polysemanticity classifications depend on activation range or explanation scoring.

rows.subject: human raters (MTurk participants)
rows.size_stated: 323 crowdsourced participants overall; 50 participants per reference-image condition
rows.operation_detail: Participants chose which of two occluded query images would retain stronger InceptionV1 channel activation, given synthetic feature visualizations as references.
rows.measure: Human accuracy on the occlusion-prediction task
rows.note: This measures human prediction of an intervention's effect, not whether the channel responds to unrelated inputs.
rows.check: This row measures human task accuracy, not neuron polysemanticity. The abstract gives 68±4% for synthetic references while Section 4.1 gives 67±4%, so the value is inconsistent across the paper.
